Guernica. Pablo Picasso's monumental 1937 anti-war mural painting depicts the bombing of the Basque town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War. Rendered in fractured, anguished forms and stark black-and-white palette, it stands as one of the most powerful artistic responses to violence and suffering ever created, transforming personal tragedy into universal protest.

Completed in 1937 for the Spanish Pavilion at the Paris International Exposition, it was commissioned in response to the bombing of Guernica by Nationalist forces. The painting measures over 11 feet tall and nearly 27 feet wide, a monumental scale that amplifies its emotional and political force. It depicts fragmented human and animal forms: a weeping mother, a bull, a horse pierced by a lance, dismembered limbs, all arranged in cubist distortion to convey chaos and agony.

Picasso used only black, white, and gray, emphasizing the starkness of death and the totality of loss. The bull and horse serve as ambiguous symbols, sometimes read as Spain and fascism, sometimes as brutality and innocence, or as matador and victim. The work became an iconic symbol of artistic opposition to war and inspired countless anti-war artworks across the twentieth century.
